title: Sales intelligence platforms for CPG brands: a buyer's guide
summary: A buyer's guide to sales intelligence platforms for CPG brands: prospecting databases vs. account signals, what to check in a demo, and eight questions to ask.
body_markdown:
Search for "sales intelligence platform" and you'll get long lists of tools, mostly written by the companies that sell them. Nearly all of them cover the first job. That's fair enough if you sell software to other businesses, but it won't help much if you run sales at a CPG brand.


I learned this the hard way at Better Nature. We scaled to roughly 5,000 stores across six countries. The question that kept me up at night was never "who do I call at a chain we're not in yet?" It was "which of the stores we're already in has quietly stopped reordering?" Most of the time I found out weeks too late, from a rep visit or a distributor report that landed after the shelf space had gone to someone else.


## What does a sales intelligence platform do?


A sales intelligence platform collects data about companies and buyers, then tells your sales team who to contact and what to say. Most tools in the category run on the same inputs: contact details, company information (often called firmographics), signs that a company is researching a purchase (buyer intent), and updates to your CRM, like Salesforce or HubSpot.


That's the first job, finding people at companies you've never sold to. The second job is knowing what's happening inside the accounts you already have. Almost every tool in the category is built for the first one.


Two terms help keep them apart. A *prospecting database* sells access to contact and company records, so your reps can reach people they don't know yet. ZoomInfo, Apollo, Cognism, and Lusha all work this way. *Account signals* are changes in how an existing customer is buying, like an order that didn't arrive, a product that left the shelf, or a delivery that came in short.


Sales intelligence also gets mixed up with three other kinds of tools. A CRM stores your contacts, deals, and notes. A sales engagement tool sends your email sequences. And a conversation intelligence tool like Gong records your sales calls and analyzes them.


*Most sales intelligence platforms do the first job. A CPG brand selling through distributors mostly needs the second.*


## Why CPG is different: you already know your accounts


If you sell through distributors and retailers, you already know who your accounts are. You know which chains carry you, which DSD houses deliver you, and which UNFI and KeHE warehouses ship you. What you don't know on a Monday morning is which of those accounts is slowing down, and a contact database can't tell you, because that information sits with your distributors and retailers.


That's true whether you sell through wholesalers, broadliners like UNFI and KeHE, or DSD distributors, since in every case the store's sales data lives in someone else's system. It matters less for your own online store. And if you're still looking for your first retail buyers, a contact database is exactly what you need (I cover when that's the case inthe section on prospecting databases ).


### Where a CPG brand's data lives


Distributor depletions show what a distributor sold to stores, which is a different number from what you shipped to the distributor. CLEAN Cause gets its DSD depletions every day through VIP. The UNFI and KeHE portals report weekly,[retailer portals](https://corvera.ai/use-cases/retailer-portal-data) report on their own schedule, and reps keep their own notes in shared spreadsheets.


Each of those sources uses a different name for the same store. At CLEAN Cause, KeHE calls a chain an "area name" and VIP calls it an "immediate owner." When a store moves from one distributor to another, it can look like a lost customer in one report and a brand-new one in the next, which means nobody can say which accounts are at risk until the names are matched.


### How CLEAN Cause uses this data


CLEAN Cause sells organic energy drinks through about thirty DSD distributors, dozens of UNFI and KeHE warehouses, and retailers including Whole Foods and HEB. Its data came from eight sources, each in its own format, and two regional distributors sent their reports as email attachments.


On Corvera, nearly 8,000 stores were matched across those sources, so a store that changes distributor keeps one record. Reports that used to be rebuilt every month now update every day.


Jon Sowers, their VP of Sales, built a daily dashboard on top of it. It shows which accounts to call and what to ask for, puts a dollar value on each risk and opportunity, and flags products missing from stores in chains CLEAN Cause already sells to. It flagged $250K of sales opportunities.


Todd Bondy, CLEAN Cause's CEO, put the problem better than I can: "Data isn't our constraint. We have more data than we know what to do with. Putting it in usable formats in order to drive actions is the constraint."


You can read the full story in[how CLEAN Cause runs its daily call list](https://corvera.ai/case-studies/clean-cause) .


*A CPG brand's accounts are known, but each feed names them differently, so the first job of sales intelligence for a brand is matching them.*


## What a CPG brand needs from a sales intelligence platform


Most buyer's guides judge these tools on data accuracy, privacy compliance (GDPR), and how well they sync with your CRM. Those matter for a contact database. For a brand selling through distributors, I'd ask something simpler: can the tool tell you something new about a store you already sell to? I'd check five things in a demo.


### It connects to your distributor and portal data


Ask which data sources it connects to today, by name. That means VIP or direct distributor depletions, the UNFI and KeHE portals, your retailer portals, and your rep spreadsheets. A tool that only reads your CRM can only see what your team typed in, so your distributors' numbers never reach it.


### It keeps one record per store


Every source names stores differently. If a store that switches distributor shows up as a lost customer, your lost-account numbers will be wrong and your reps will chase stores that never left. Ask how the tool matches stores across sources, who approves the matches, and whether the store's history moves with it. On Corvera, this matching happens in[the context layer](https://corvera.ai/product) , and your team approves each match.


### It shows changes at store and product level


Useful signals are specific, like[a store that hasn't ordered in five weeks](https://corvera.ai/use-cases/unsold-accounts) ,[a chain that carries three of your nine SKUs](https://corvera.ai/use-cases/distribution-gaps) , or a warehouse that shipped fewer cases than were ordered. A monthly report tends to surface these after the shelf space is gone. You want them daily, while your rep still has time to act.


### It tells your reps who to call first


Hand a rep a list of four hundred slowing stores and they'll do what I did at Better Nature. They'll pick the handful they recognize and hope the rest are fine. What works is a short list of[today's most important calls](https://corvera.ai/use-cases/sales#sales-enablement) , each with the reason and what to ask for, so a rep can get through it the same day.


### Your team approves what goes out


Some tools draft messages for your team, such as a brief for the rep, an email to the buyer, or a follow-up to the distributor. Ask who approves each one before it's sent, and where that approval is recorded. On Corvera, scheduled agents draft these messages, and your team approves the store matches they're based on. There's more on how that works in[sales intelligence for CPG sales teams](https://corvera.ai/use-cases/sales#sales-intelligence) .
